title: Power and sample size
dek: Power is P(reject H₀ | a specific alternative, a design, a test). It is not P(H₁ | star) and not a number you compute after seeing p = 0.06.
story: Fix a test, a Type I level α, a design (n, blocks, clusters), and a scientifically interesting alternative θ₁. Power is the probability of rejection when θ = θ₁. 80% is a convention, not a law of nature. Underpowered studies of a real effect mostly produce noisy estimates, not “proof of absence.”

Sample-size formulas from NIST and public-domain texts are inverted power calculations for simple Gaussian or binomial two-sample tests. They need an effect size in scientific units, a variance, and α. Inventing all three after the data exist is p-hacking’s cousin, post hoc power — a one-to-one function of the p-value, not new information.

Clustered TB trials, rare mutations, and FDR across a genome change the arithmetic. Effective n is closer to the number of independent clusters or independent lineages. Bonferroni or BH spends α; power at a given alternative falls. Compute that, do not only compute a two-sample t as if you had iid people and one test.
deepTitle: The operating curve, and clustered n
deep: Gaussian two-sample, equal n, known σ: n per arm ≈ 2 (z_{1−α/2} + z_{power})² σ² / δ² for a difference δ. Unknown σ replaces z with t and iterates. Binary outcomes use a similar sketch with p(1−p) in place of σ², or simulation from a GLM.
Minimal detectable effect: invert the formula for δ given n. That is often the more honest grant sentence than “we will have 80% power for an OR of 1.05 with 40 isolates.”
Random effects: if ICC = ρ, design effect ≈ 1 + (m−1)ρ for clusters of size m. Divide naive n by that. A household trial that ignores this is not 180 independent people.
Bayesian design uses a different operating characteristic (e.g. expected width of a posterior interval, or decision risk). Still needs a design alternative or a prior over θ. Still not post hoc.

formulas.label: Two-sample Gaussian n (sketch)
formulas.note: δ = mean difference you care about. Not the observed difference after the study.

visual.caption: Power as overlapping sampling laws of a test statistic: a null-centred law and an alternative-centred law. The rejection cut is fixed by α under the null. The area of the alternative law beyond that cut is power. Post hoc power redraws this with δ̂, which is circular.

example.title: Household ICC eats your n
example.setup: Want 80% power, α = 0.05 two-sided, binary outcome, risk difference 0.10, p ≈ 0.2, σ² ≈ 0.16. Naive two-sample n_arm ≈ 2 (1.96+0.84)² (0.16)/0.01 ≈ 251. Households of m = 4, ρ = 0.1.

steps.title: Naive
steps.body: About 250 people per arm if iid. You do not have iid.

steps.title: DEFF
steps.body: 1 + (4−1)×0.1 = 1.3. Need about 30% more people, or equivalently fewer independent households than you thought.

steps.title: Grant sentence
steps.body: Power is computed at RD = 0.10 with ICC 0.1, 4 members, two-sided 5%. If the scientific δ is 0.03, this design is a precision study, not an 80% power study — say that.

example.takeaway: Power lives at a named alternative and a named design. Clusters and multiple tests rewrite n.

check.prompt: Post hoc power computed from the observed effect and the observed p-value:
choices: Is independent information about whether the study was large enough
Is essentially a recoding of the p-value, not a design calculation at a pre-specified δ
check.answer: Is essentially a recoding of the p-value, not a design calculation at a pre-specified δ
check.why: Observed power is a monotone function of |T|. It does not rescue p = 0.06.

whyWrong.Is independent information about whether: It is not independent of the result.

check.why: 1 + 4×0.2 = 1.8. You need 1.8 times as many people as the iid formula.

check.prompt: On the power density plate, the tiny-shift curve sits almost on the null. That picture is:
check.figureHint: Three laws of a test statistic; one barely shifted.
choices: High power for that tiny θ
Low power: most of the alternative law still misses the α cut drawn under the null
check.answer: Low power: most of the alternative law still misses the α cut drawn under the null
check.why: Power is the alternative area beyond the null cut. A tiny shift leaves little of that area.

whyWrong.Proof that α was 80%: α is the null tail, not power.
whyWrong.A posterior under H₁: These are sampling laws of a statistic.
